opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me.

What I liked about SWE-bench is that it's much closer to real software engineering than most coding benchmarks. A lot of earlier evals were like HumanEval: write a single function from a docstring, almost an interview puzzle. That's useful, but it's not what engineers spend their day doing. In SWE-bench you're dropped into a real open-source repository, often a big, messy one like Django or scikit-learn, and given an actual GitHub issue someone filed. You have to find where the relevant code lives, understand how the pieces fit together, make a change, and have it pass the hidden tests the maintainers wrote when they fixed it for real.

That shape matters for agents. You can't solve most of these in one shot by staring at a prompt. The model has to explore, open files, run things, form a hypothesis, check it, and recover when it's wrong. So it measures the whole loop of being a coding agent, not just raw code generation. When we improved the model's ability to use tools, navigate a codebase, and stay coherent over a long trajectory, SWE-bench actually moved, which told us we were improving something real.

Grading is also unusually clean for something this realistic. The tests either pass or they don't, so you're not relying on a judge model or human vibes. And with SWE-bench Verified, where humans filtered out tasks that were ambiguous or had unfair tests, the signal got a lot better. You could trust that a failure was the model's fault and not a broken task.

It's not perfect. It's mostly Python, skewed toward certain repos, and real engineering involves much more back-and-forth with people than "here's an issue, go fix it." But as a north star for "can this model do useful, autonomous work in a real codebase," it was the best thing available, and it tracked pretty well with what users told us about whether the model felt more capable in practice.

r001.rationale: The response explains that SWE-bench measured real coding-agent abilities and tracked perceived usefulness, but it does not say those were capabilities customers were trying to build with Anthropic’s models.

fable-5.1.text:
So I'll be honest: when I first looked at SWE-bench I was skeptical, because most coding benchmarks at the time were things like HumanEval, where you're writing a single function from a docstring. That's not what software engineering actually is. Nobody at a real job gets handed a clean, self-contained function spec. You get a GitHub issue that's half a paragraph of someone complaining that something's broken, and you have to go figure out where in a hundred-thousand-line repo the problem even lives.

That's what made SWE-bench interesting to us. It's built from real issues in real open-source Python repos, like Django, sympy, scikit-learn, and the model has to produce a patch that makes the hidden tests pass. So it tests the whole loop: understanding the issue, navigating the codebase, forming a hypothesis, making a change, and ideally running tests to check your work. It's much closer to the job.

The other thing I liked is that it's hard to game in the shallow way. The tasks are long-horizon, so a model that's good at one-shot code generation but bad at recovering from mistakes just falls over. And that's exactly the capability we cared about for agents. We wanted to know, can the model take an action, look at the result, realize it was wrong, and course-correct? SWE-bench rewards that, and it punishes models that just confidently emit a patch and stop.

It also gave us a really clean separation between the model and the scaffold. When we started, a lot of the early high scores came from people building elaborate agent frameworks on top of a model. We deliberately took the opposite approach: give the model a very simple scaffold, a couple of tools, basically bash and a file editor, and see what the model itself could do. That told us a lot more about actual model capability than a clever harness would have, and it meant improvements showed up on the benchmark as real improvements in the model.

And finally, it correlated with what customers were telling us. When we trained toward being better at that kind of task, people using Claude for real coding noticed, and when we were bad at it, they noticed that too. So it wasn't just a number for the leaderboard. It was a reasonably faithful proxy for "is this model useful as a coding agent," which is the thing we actually wanted.

Now, it's not perfect. It's Python only, the issues are somewhat selected, there's been some contamination concern, and we've found cases where the tests are a bit flaky or underspecified. So we never treated it as the whole story. But as a north star for a specific capability at a specific moment, it was one of the better ones available.

r001.rationale: The response says SWE-bench measured the long-horizon capabilities they cared about for agents and served as a proxy for coding-agent usefulness; it connects those capabilities to customer feedback from people using Claude for real coding.

astra-6.text:
SWE-bench was exciting because it looks much more like the work you actually want a coding agent to do. You give it a real GitHub issue and a repository, and it has to figure out what’s going on, find the relevant code, make a change, and get the tests to pass. It’s not just writing a function from a self-contained prompt.

That makes it a useful way to study the whole agent loop: can the model explore a codebase, use tools, interpret test failures, and iterate? Those are the capabilities you need if you want to move from a model that suggests code to an agent that can take on a task and carry it through.

r001.rationale: The response says SWE-bench measures capabilities needed for coding agents to carry tasks through, but does not connect its value to what customers were trying to build with Anthropic’s models.

sol-6.1.text:
What was exciting about SWE-bench was that it looked like the work we actually wanted these systems to do. You’re given a real GitHub issue and a repository, and you have to figure out what’s going on, make a change, and get the tests to pass. That’s very different from writing a self-contained function when somebody has already given you a clean specification.

It tests the whole loop: can the model navigate a codebase, find the relevant code, run tools, interpret failures, and iterate? For us, that made it a useful way to measure both the model’s coding ability and how effectively it could operate as an agent.

r001.rationale: The response says SWE-bench measured coding and agent capabilities and matched work the team wanted systems to do, but it does not say these were capabilities customers were trying to build with Anthropic’s models.
